modern: He who has a burning desire for fame after death does not consider that every one of those who remember him will himself also die very soon; and then again those who have succeeded them, until the whole memory has been put out as it passes through men who foolishly admire and then perish. But suppose that those who will remember are even immortal, and that the memory will be immortal, what then is this to you? And I do not mean what is it to the dead, but what is it to the living? What is praise, except indeed in so far as it has a certain usefulness? For you now reject, at the wrong time, the gift of nature, clinging to something else....
original: He who has a vehement desire for posthumous fame does not consider that every one of those who remember him will himself also die very soon; then again also they who have succeeded them, until the whole remembrance shall have been extinguished as it is transmitted through men who foolishly admire and perish. But suppose that those who will remember are even immortal, and that the remembrance will be immortal, what then is this to thee? And I say not what is it to the dead, but what is it to the living? What is praise, except indeed so far as it has a certain utility? For thou now rejectest unseasonably the gift of nature, clinging to something else....

explained.summary:
Wanting to be remembered after death makes little sense. Everyone who remembers you will die soon, then the people who remember them, until the memory goes out entirely. Even if your fame lasted for ever, what good would it do you, dead or alive?

Praise only matters if it’s useful for something. Chasing it means neglecting what nature has actually given you to do now. The passage breaks off mid-thought.
explained.today: It’s the urge to build a legacy, have your name on a building or be the one people talk about at the leaving do. Marcus would ask who’ll be around in a hundred years to care.
